name: Classical Quechua
confidence_why: González Holguín 1607 gives stress on the penultimate syllable for the Cuzco-based colonial standard, and Itier 2013 and Adelaar & Muysken 2004 accept that as the Quechua norm, but the other colonial grammar filed under this language, Santo Tomás 1560, describes a variety in which suffixed words keep the stem's stress and some trisyllables are stressed on the first syllable, which Itier 2013 reads as an earlier stage and Adelaar & Muysken 2004 as a deviant coastal dialect, so the penultimate rule holds for the standard variety only.

new_statements.quote: Final stress is a characteristic of the first-person marker -'y. Otherwise, penultimate stress is predominant. More complex, non-penultimate stress patterns, involving word-initial stress and stress dependent on syllable structure, are found in QI Ancash and in QI Cajatambo (cf. Torero 1964: 461; Parker 1976). The northern Peruvian dialects QIIA Ferreñafe (Escribens 1977) and QIIB Amazonas (Taylor 1975; Chaparro 1985) also have deviant stress patterns, as had the sixteenth-century coastal dialect described by Santo Tomás.

new_statements.relation_note: Partial contradiction, placement unspecified. The catalog records fixed penultimate stress for Classical Quechua. The book agrees that penultimate stress is the Quechua default, but states that the sixteenth-century coastal variety described by Santo Tomás (1560), which Glottolog lists as a source of clas1251, had a deviant (non-penultimate) stress pattern; it does not say what that pattern was. It is silent on the stress of the seventeenth-century Cuzco-based standard (Holguín 1607). Queries for 'classical Quechua', 'Quechua stress', 'stress in Quechua', 'stress rule(s)', 'paroxytone', 'oxytone', 'stressed syllable' and Santo Tomás + stress/accent returned nothing further. new_statements.rule_in_words: Across Quechua, penultimate stress is the predominant pattern; the only colonial variety the book mentions for stress, Santo Tomás's sixteenth-century 'coastal' dialect (the 1560 Grammatica/Lexicon, which Glottolog files under clas1251), is said to have had a 'deviant', i.e. non-penultimate, stress pattern, but the book gives no placement for it and says nothing about the stress of the Cuzco-based colonial standard (González Holguín 1607, Huarochirí manuscript).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned for any Quechua variety.
new_statements.exceptions: Pacaraos Quechua: phonemic final-vs-penultimate contrast, final stress on the first-person marker -y, otherwise penultimate; word-final stress in Pacaraos, Tarma and northern Junín from elision of a final syllable; quantity-insensitive Ancash and quantity-insensitive Cajatambo: word-initial stress and stress dependent on syllable structure; Huaraz (Torero 1964): a non-final long syllable (CVC, CV:) is stressed, otherwise the first syllable or a final syllable with a long vowel; northern Peruvian QIIA Ferreñafe and QIIB Amazonas and Santo Tomás's sixteenth-century coastal dialect: 'deviant stress patterns' (no detail); a penultimate-to-initial shift in some northern Peruvian dialects; footnote 24: whether an Ancash-type accentuation reflects Proto-Quechua is debated, the authors arguing from the 'essentially penultimate stress of Pacaraos Quechua'.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog clas1251 'Classical Quechua' bundles the colonial lengua general: Santo Tomás 1560 (the 'coastal'/central sixteenth-century variety), González Holguín 1607 (Cuzco-based standard) and Itier's 2010 edition of Espinosa Medrano (seventeenth-century Cuzco). Adelaar & Muysken's stress statement concerns only the first of these (Santo Tomás's coastal dialect, 'deviant stress'); their general 'penultimate stress is predominant' is a pan-Quechua statement made in the context of Pacaraos Quechua (a modern quantity-insensitive/QII-intermediate dialect of Lima department), not of any colonial variety.

new_statements.quote: In most Quechua dialects stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel of each polysyllabic word form and thus provides an easy phonology-based criterion for word delimitation. [...] The northern Peruvian dialects QIIA Ferreñafe (Escribens 1977) and QIIB Amazonas (Taylor 1975; Chaparro 1985) also have deviant stress patterns, as had the sixteenth-century coastal dialect described by Santo Tomás. [...] [fn. 24] Whether or not an Ancash-type accentuation pattern reflects that of Proto-Quechua is a matter of debate. Against this view, advocated by Torero (1964), we may argue that the essentially penultimate stress of Pacaraos Quechua [...] is likely to have been inherited from Proto-Quechua.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The book gives no stress rule for Classical Quechua (the colonial lengua general / Cuzco standard of Gonzalez Holguin 1607) as such. It states that in most Quechua dialects stress falls on the penultimate vowel of every polysyllabic word (word-final only in interjections/emphatics and, in quantity-insensitive, on a word-final first-person long vowel), argues in fn. 24 that essentially penultimate stress was probably inherited from Proto-Quechua, and says that the sixteenth-century 'coastal' dialect described by Santo Tomas (1560) had a 'deviant' (i.e. non-penultimate) stress pattern, without saying what that pattern was. A full-text scan of the whole Quechua chapter (pp. 179-263) for stress/accent and of the book for Santo Tomas / Gonzalez Holguin / lengua general finds nothing further on colonial-period stress: Holguin is discussed only for relative clauses (pp. 17-18) and as a bibliographic landmark (p. 191).
new_statements.exceptions: word-final stress in interjections and emphatic expressions (alaláw); in Tarma/northern Junin after elision of a final syllable; in quantity-insensitive when the first-person long-vowel morpheme is word-final; Pacaraos phonemic final vs penult stress (first-person -´y, elided suffixes); non-penultimate, partly weight/initial patterns in quantity-insensitive Ancash (Huaraz rule after Torero 1964), quantity-insensitive Cajatambo, QIIA Ferreñafe, QIIB Amazonas, and the 16th-c. coastal dialect of Santo Tomas (pattern unspecified).
new_statements.identity_note: Adelaar and Muysken do not use the label 'Classical Quechua'. The relevant remarks concern (a) Quechua dialects in general, (b) the sixteenth-century 'coastal' dialect / lengua general described by Santo Tomas 1560 (which they assign to Quechua IIB, pp. 187, 191), and (c) Gonzalez Holguin's 1607 grammar of the Cuzco-based lengua general (mentioned pp. 17-18, 191 without any stress statement). Glottolog's clas1251 covers both colonial descriptions.

readall_conflicts: Adelaar & Muysken 2004 (p. 207) support penultimate stress as the Quechua default (and, in fn. 24, argue that Pacaraos's 'essentially penultimate stress' is the older pattern), which agrees with the catalog's penultimate rule for Classical Quechua. But the same sentence says that 'the sixteenth-century coastal dialect described by Santo Tomás' had 'deviant stress patterns', without giving the placement. Since Glottolog's clas1251 includes Santo Tomás's 1560 grammar and dictionary among its sources, the catalog's uniform penultimate rule is not supported by this book for that colonial variety; the book is silent on the Cuzco-based colonial standard (González Holguín 1607, Espinosa Medrano, Huarochirí manuscript), which is the core of what 'Classical Quechua' usually denotes. No source opened gives an alternative placement, so the conflict is a flag (one colonial variety deviates, placement unknown), not a competing rule. One partial disagreement, already held by the project and unchanged by the full read: the catalog record (classification conflict) codes Classical Quechua as fixed penultimate on the strength of Gonzalez Holguin 1607 (explicit: 'no hay acentos en la ultima silaba sino en la penultima') and Santo Tomas 1560. Adelaar and Muysken 2004 (p. 207) say the sixteenth-century coastal dialect described by Santo Tomas had a 'deviant' stress pattern, grouping it with the non-penultimate systems of Ancash, Cajatambo, Ferreñafe and Amazonas, but do not say where stress fell…

sources.quote: '5. Una regularización del régimen acentual que llevó a una generalización de la acentuación en la penúltima sílaba. En efecto, el sistema acentual complejo del quechua descrito por Domingo de Santo Tomás correspondía probablemente al cuzqueño antiguo, pues encontramos hoy sus huellas en algunos dialectos ecuatorianos.' I.e. Santo Tomas (complex, non-penult) vs Holguin/Third-Council (generalized penult) is read as a diachronic change c. 1550-1600, not two coexisting descriptions of one system.

tone.quote: Pitch or tone plays no role in either of the two modern dialects with which we are concerned. Tone is not used to make phonemic distinctions and intonation is used to distinguish phrase types only by speakers under marked Spanish influence. The phrase type is properly indicated by the use of appropriate suffixes and the Spanish (and English) use of intonation sounds ludicrous to native speakers of Inca. ... 10 My field data on Inca tone patterns are insufficient for a more detailed statement in this paper.
